passage:
Counsellor’s note, Thursday. Wasim came in after lunch and sat with his bag on his lap. Three weeks ago he reported a lab-marks entry that had been changed, and the lab in-charge corrected it. Since then the class chat has stopped including him, someone wrote “informer” on the lab board, and two groups go quiet when he passes.
He said, “I keep thinking I should have said nothing.” He also said Samir, who sits beside him, still shares notes and eats lunch with him, and that this helps.
I told Wasim that reporting was not his fault and that the isolation is what needs dealing with. That afternoon I spoke to the head of department about the board and the chat. The head had the board wiped before the last class and said the class chat will be raised with the whole group tomorrow.
Next week I will meet Wasim again.
— College counsellor

qa.q: What did someone write on the lab board?
qa.a: Someone wrote “informer” on the lab board.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when he said he should have said nothing?
qa.a: Wasim was feeling lonely and doubtful about having reported, since he was being shut out by the class. It shows the isolation weighs heavily on him.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do that helped Wasim?
qa.a: The counsellor told Wasim that reporting was not his fault and took the board and the chat to the head of department that same afternoon. They also planned another meeting for next week.

qa.q: How might Samir's sitting beside Wasim matter to Wasim?
qa.a: Samir's sharing notes and eating lunch together shows Wasim is not alone. One ally can make the labelling and gossip easier to bear.

grounding: Shows a student isolated and labelled after reporting wrongdoing, with one ally and a counsellor's same-day action.

passage:
Thursday night. The whole class went quiet when I walked in. I reported the changed marks on Monday, and today nobody saved me a seat and my name was left off the project group. Somebody drew a rat on my notebook.
In the canteen I sat alone until Mahima put her tray down across from me and said, “I think you did the right thing.” She didn’t say anything else. I nearly cried into my tea.
I keep asking myself whether I’m a troublemaker. I’m still angry and scared. Tomorrow I’m going to show the counsellor the drawing. At least one person is on my side.
— Baljeet

qa.q: What did Mahima say to Baljeet in the canteen?
qa.a: Mahima said, “I think you did the right thing.”

qa.q: Why did Baljeet nearly cry into the tea?
qa.a: Baljeet had felt shut out all day, and one kind sentence from Mahima showed someone was on Baljeet's side. Relief and loneliness came together.

qa.q: What is Baljeet planning to do about the rat drawing, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Baljeet plans to show the counsellor the drawing. Telling an adult who can act helps the retaliation stop.

qa.q: What might Mahima have been feeling when she sat down at Baljeet's table?
qa.a: Mahima may have felt nervous about being seen with Baljeet but decided to be kind anyway. Saying so quietly and only once suggests a careful, brave gesture.

grounding: Shows a student who reported wrongdoing being isolated, gossiped about and labelled, and helped by one ally.
